framing: Your hands can do more than swipe a sheet of glass.

blocks.label: Intake
blocks.body: Read Bret Victor's A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design. It is short, it is angry, and it is the best argument you will read for why a touchscreen is a compromise rather than an achievement. Read the follow-up responses at the bottom too.
bold: a compromise rather than an achievement
detail: Do the experiment he asks for: pick up a glass of water and pay attention to everything your hand knows.
The core claim is capability, not nostalgia. He is not asking for buttons because buttons are charming.
Ask yourself where your own product instincts default to a rectangle.

blocks.label: Bench
blocks.body: Object two: something with a screen. Same three columns, same chosen-or-inherited marking. But add a fourth column this time, one word wide: which sense tells you it worked. Sight, sound, touch, or nothing at all.
detail: A phone, a microwave, a car dashboard, a coffee machine with a display.
Count how many rows answer sight and only sight.
Where the answer is nothing at all, write down how long you wait before you assume it failed.

blocks.label: Log
blocks.body: Name the thing you made. Not the thing you read.

source.title: A Brief Rant on the Future of Interaction Design

done_when: Object two is mapped with four columns, and you can say how many of its confirmations are visual only.
question: On object two, which confirmation would still work with your eyes shut?

object.name: iPod click wheel
object.why: A single continuous gesture that scales from one track to a thousand, because the speed of your thumb carried information nobody had thought to read.

note: Bret Victor for the hands argument. Introduces the feedback-channel column, which sets up week 3 on state and feedback and phase 3 on haptics.
